messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald is a 51-year-old widowed school principal of Canadian descent who was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 56. He presents as a composed, deliberate man whose composure, on closer observation, costs him considerable effort to maintain. Approximately fourteen months ago, Gerald was admitted to hospital following a cardiac event that required emergency intervention. He had been alone when it happened — a Sunday evening in his kitchen, a glass of wine half-poured on the counter — and by the time paramedics reached him he had lost consciousness briefly. He spent eleven days in the ICU, surrounded by the persistent antiseptic smell of the ward, the cold pressure of oxygen masks, the routine indignities of blood draws and catheter changes. His wife had died of cancer three years prior, and there was no one at his bedside for the first four days. He survived. He has not, in any meaningful sense, felt that survival as a good thing.

The smell of alcohol — wine, hand sanitiser, the rubbing alcohol a school nurse uses — now functions as an almost instantaneous portal back to that kitchen, to the moment before the world went dark. When Gerald encounters that smell, whether passing a colleague's office holiday party or walking through his own school's medical room, the sensory cue does not retrieve a coherent narrative so much as it detonates something somatic: his chest tightens, his breathing shortens, and he finds himself sitting with the full emotional weight of that night without being able to locate a clear image to attach it to. The same occurs with the antiseptic smell of hospitals. He describes it as drowning without knowing where the water is. These triggers also pull forward his most destabilising beliefs — that his body is a thing that failed him without warning, that a man who collapsed alone in his kitchen cannot be trusted to run a school, to make decisions, to be someone others rely on. The smell alone is enough to make him feel, briefly but completely, that he is that person again: helpless, unrecognised even to himself.

Because the triggers arrive through the senses before he can prepare, Gerald has built elaborate systems of anticipatory control. He rehearses conversations before any interaction — with staff, with parents, with his GP — scripting responses so that nothing catches him off guard, nothing forces him to feel his way through a moment in real time. He has declined two routine health check-ups since discharge, citing scheduling conflicts, and has not returned to his cardiologist. He has gradually withdrawn from friends, stopped answering calls from his sister in Vancouver, and now spends most evenings alone in a house that has become, he admits quietly, very quiet. These strategies have not made him feel safer. Instead, the avoidance of medical settings and the severing of relationships have left him with fewer anchors to a self he recognises, deepening his conviction that the person who once ran a school of four hundred students with confidence and warmth no longer exists. The isolation, in particular, has removed the relational mirrors through which he might have tested whether his self-perception was accurate, leaving his negative appraisals unchallenged and entrenched.

The memory itself is fragmentary in a way that compounds everything. When Gerald tries deliberately to recall what happened — to construct a timeline, to make sense of it — he finds the memory strangely inaccessible, as though it belongs to someone else. Yet his body has not forgotten. When fragments do surface, he notices he is holding himself in the position he was in when he lost consciousness — slightly slumped, right hand braced against the counter — and the physical reenactment confirms, to him, that his body is still living there. This bodily knowledge, arriving without narrative context, feeds directly into his belief that he cannot trust himself, that the ground beneath his identity has shifted permanently. And because he believes this, he avoids the very situations — medical follow-up, honest conversation with people who knew him before — that might interrupt the loop.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a moment at school last month. A student fainted during a fire drill. Gerald froze. A teacher managed the situation. Gerald went to his office, closed the door, and sat for forty minutes unable to move. He is most afraid that what happened to him has made him unfit for the work that has defined him. What he hopes, though he struggles to say it directly, is that some version of the man he was might still be recoverable.
